To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a higher frequency of MAIT cell and lower iNKT cell frequency at age 1 y is associated with protection against the development of asthma in inner-city children.
MAIT cell frequency and iNKT cell activity in dust samples are associated with reduced risk of childhood asthma, possibly by promoting a Th1 response.
MAIT cell frequency and iNKT cell activity in the home environment may be associated with protection from childhood asthma.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of innate-like T cell subsets in the development of asthma in inner-city children and the possible influence of the home environment on these cells.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the innate-like T cell response in the first year of life is important to asthma risk, but it may not be the innate-like T cells themselves that are the critical players.

the presence of MAIT cells in early childhood may protect against asthma, whereas the presence of iNKT cell activity may be a biomarker of increased exposure to microbes and therefore protection against asthma.
